title: The Island and the Nile: Guénon from the Loire to the Cairo Necropolis
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Loire and the Sickly Child

stops.name: Blois, birth on the Loire
stops.date_confidence: attested; both Wikipedias give 15 November 1886. The street and the house are not named in any source consulted, so the pin is the town.
stops.campa: René-Jean-Marie-Joseph Guénon is born at Blois, in a devout Catholic household on the middle Loire; his father is an architect. The child is fragile from the first week, and much of the rearing passes to an aunt, Madame Duru, in a village downriver. Blois is a cathedral town of some twenty thousand: a château, a bridge, a market. He will live inside it for eighteen years and leave it once, for good. What he read there, and when the metaphysics began, no source records.
suggested_refs: Blois parish and civil registers for November 1886, not consulted in this pass

stops.name: Montlivault, the aunt who raises him
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the year; French Wikipedia attests the aunt and the decades of visits but dates neither the start nor any single stay. The visits stop around 1928.
stops.campa: Ten kilometres down the Loire from Blois, and six from the roofs of Chambord, the village of Montlivault holds the house of Madame Duru. A boy too ill for a normal childhood is sent here and kept here, and the habit outlasts the illness: Guénon comes back to this aunt for thirty-five years, from Paris, from the years of the reviews and the lodges, until about 1928. The house has no address in the sources. The village is where he will also be married, twenty years on.
suggested_refs: The Duru house at Montlivault, unlocated by street address

stops.name: Blois, the schoolyard on the avenue de Châteaudun
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1902-1903 (baccalauréat) and 1903-1904 (mathématiques élémentaires) by French Wikipedia; the calendar year 1902 is chosen as the anchor.
stops.campa: Guénon takes his baccalauréat at the school on the avenue de Châteaudun, named for the historian Augustin Thierry since 1872, and stays a further year for the classe de mathématiques élémentaires. He is good at mathematics in the way that will matter later: not as a career but as a grammar, the one European discipline he will keep quoting after he has renounced the rest. In the autumn of 1904 he goes up to Paris for mathématiques spéciales. The lycée now carries a different name.
suggested_refs: Cité scolaire Augustin-Thierry, 13 avenue de Châteaudun, Blois; the lycée renamed Robert-Badinter in January 2025

stops.name: Paris, the Collège Rollin on the avenue Trudaine
stops.date_confidence: attested 1904-1906 by French Wikipedia's education infobox. The incoming research pool dated the arrival to 1905; that was wrong, and its own geography lens contradicted it.
stops.campa: He arrives in the autumn of 1904 at the lycée on the avenue Trudaine, then called the Collège Rollin, to prepare the entrance competitions of the Polytechnique and the École normale supérieure. Mathematics in the morning, philosophy after. It is the only time in his life he spends inside the machinery that manufactures French intellectuals, and it is the machinery he will spend forty years describing as a mill for grinding quality into quantity. He is seventeen and has left Blois for good.
suggested_refs: Lycée Jacques-Decour, avenue Trudaine, Paris IX, formerly Collège Rollin

stops.name: Paris, the room on the rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Île
stops.date_confidence: attested from 1905 by French Wikipedia; the building number is not given for this first lodging. The military discharge for poor health is undated in both Wikipedias, and the sources place it either here or in the Sorbonne years.
stops.campa: Health breaks the plan. In 1905 Guénon abandons the preparation for the two great competitions, and the army discharges him on the same grounds. At nineteen every institutional door in France closes at once. He takes a room on the rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Île, choosing the quiet island over the crowded Latin Quarter, and keeps an address on that street for a quarter of a century. Everything he writes will be written from outside the university, which will examine him and never employ him.
suggested_refs: The rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Île, Paris IV; the specific building unrecorded in the sources consulted

stops.name: Paris, the circle of Papus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the coordinate is a placeholder with no source behind it. The affiliation with Papus's milieu from 1905 and the expulsion from the Martinist Order in 1909 are both attested; the meeting place is not named anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: The student with no future in mathematics falls in with Gérard Encausse, the physician who signs himself Papus, and with the Martinist order he runs. Paris in 1905 has a whole economy of these: lodges, chapters, patriarchates, degrees conferred by men who conferred them on each other. Guénon takes the degrees. In 1909 the Martinists strike him from the rolls. He learns the machinery of counterfeit initiation from the inside at twenty-two, and he will still be dismantling it at sixty.
suggested_refs: Papers of the Ordre Martiniste under Papus, 1905-1909; no meeting address identified

stops.name: Paris, 17 rue des Canettes
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia for the first session of the Ordre du Temple Rénové on 6 March 1908 and for the automatic-writing seances at 17 rue des Canettes the same year.
stops.campa: On the sixth of March the Ordre du Temple Rénové holds its first session, and at 17 rue des Canettes, a short street behind Saint-Sulpice, a young man sits at a table while a pencil moves under someone's hand and a dead Templar dictates. Six centuries earlier Jacques de Molay burned on the Île de la Cité, twenty minutes' walk east. Guénon will write seriously about the Templars later. He will also write that what happened in this room was fraud, and he will know because he was in it.
suggested_refs: 17 rue des Canettes, Paris VI, seat of the Ordre du Temple Rénové seances

stops.name: Paris, the Second Spiritualist and Masonic Congress
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia for the year and the attendance; the month follows the congress's own June dating and the venue is not specified, so the pin is the canonical Paris coordinate carried by the corpus.
stops.campa: Papus convenes a congress of spiritualists and Masons, and Guénon attends. It is a trade fair of the invisible: mesmerists, gnostic bishops, lodge officers, editors of small reviews with fewer subscribers than contributors. Here he meets Léonce Fabre des Essarts, patriarch of the Église gnostique. In this same city and this same decade Emin Arslan keeps his diplomatic rooms, and a generation earlier Helena Blavatsky passed through the identical circuit. Guénon is twenty-one and is taking notes.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the Second Spiritualist and Masonic Congress, Paris, June 1908

stops.name: Paris, the Église gnostique and the name Tau Palingenius
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the coordinate is an admitted placeholder, no rite-hall address appears in any source consulted. The affiliation and the pen-name are attested by both Wikipedias.
stops.campa: Guénon is received into the Église gnostique, founded by Jules Doinel in 1890 and led since 1900 by its patriarch Fabre des Essarts, and takes a bishop's name in it: Tau Palingenius, the born-again. The church has vestments, a synod, and almost no laity. He signs the name to everything he publishes for the next three years. Later he will insist that no European body of his lifetime held a valid initiatic chain. That verdict covers the church that has just consecrated him.
suggested_refs: The Église gnostique de France under Fabre des Essarts; no rite-hall address recorded

stops.name: Paris, La Gnose from the island
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia for the run, November 1909 to February 1912. That the review was edited from his own Île Saint-Louis address is an inference from his residence, not from a masthead.
stops.campa: From November 1909 Guénon directs a monthly review called La Gnose, writing most of it himself under the Tau Palingenius signature, out of his own rooms on the island. The circulation is negligible. The contents are not: the doctrine of the multiple states of being, the critique of Western science, the theory of cycles, all of it appears here first, in a magazine nobody reads, seven years before his first book. The apparatus of the occultist is still in place. The thought inside it has already left.
suggested_refs: Complete run of La Gnose, November 1909 to February 1912

stops.name: Paris, Ivan Aguéli and the Al Akbariyya
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a live contradiction. French Wikipedia and most scholarship put this initiation in Paris circa 1910-1912; English Wikipedia puts the same Aguéli-mediated initiation in Cairo in 1930, which is impossible because Aguéli died in 1917. The French account is followed. No meeting address is recorded.
stops.campa: A Swedish painter and anarchist called Ivan Aguéli, initiated into the Shadhiliyya at Cairo, founds a society in Paris under the name Al Akbariyya, after Ibn Arabi, whom the Sufis call the Greatest Master. Through Aguéli, Guénon is brought into the order and given the name Abd al-Wahid Yahya. He is twenty-three. He will use the name for forty years and the doctrine for the rest of his working life, and he will not set foot in a Muslim country for another seven years.
suggested_refs: The Al Akbariyya society of Ivan Aguéli, Paris; the initiatic record itself unpublished

stops.name: Paris, the Renewed Temple dissolved
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia for the dissolution in 1911 and for the closure of La Gnose in February 1912; the coordinate reuses the rue des Canettes pin of the order's own sessions.
stops.campa: The Ordre du Temple Rénové is wound up in 1911, and La Gnose stops in February of the following year. In three years Guénon has been a Martinist and struck off, a gnostic bishop, a Templar of a revived order that revived nothing, and the editor of a review that folded. Nothing he joined survived him joining it. Out of that wreckage he takes a single working principle, which he will spend the rest of his life applying: an initiation either descends from somewhere or it is theatre.
suggested_refs: Dissolution records of the Ordre du Temple Rénové, 1911

segments.name: The Marriage, the Lodge, and the War

stops.name: Montlivault, the marriage to Berthe Loury
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia for the religious ceremony at Montlivault in July 1912; English Wikipedia corroborates the year. The day is not given. The incoming research pool misfiled this wedding to Paris.
stops.campa: The gnostic bishop is married in a Catholic church, in his aunt's village, to Berthe Loury. He is twenty-five. The ceremony takes place ten kilometres from the town he was born in and a long way from every review and lodge in Paris, and it is celebrated by the church whose faith he was raised in and whose theologians will spend the next four decades deciding what to do about him. The couple returns to the rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Île. There are no children.
suggested_refs: Parish and civil marriage records, Montlivault, July 1912

stops.name: Paris, the Loge Thébah on the rue Puteaux
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. French Wikipedia gives the admission as 1910-1912 and calls the affiliation brief; the pool's geography lens said circa 1908-1909 and its chronology said 1912. The Grande Loge de France took the rue Puteaux premises in 1911, so the hall fits the later dating and not the earlier.
stops.campa: Guénon is received into the Loge Thébah of the Grande Loge de France, Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, which meets in a former Franciscan convent on the rue Puteaux in the seventeenth arrondissement. The affiliation is brief; French Wikipedia says so plainly. Half a century earlier the Emir Abdelkader, beaten by France and honoured by it, had been initiated at Alexandria by a lodge in this same country, and had walked out again on a point of doctrine. Guénon leaves too, and keeps the subject.
suggested_refs: 8 rue Puteaux, Paris XVII, premises of the Grande Loge de France from 1911

stops.name: Paris, writing as Le Sphinx
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia for the collaboration and the pseudonym from 1913; the coordinate is his own address, since no editorial address is recorded.
stops.campa: From 1913 Guénon writes for La France antimaçonnique under the name Le Sphinx, a Freemason contributing to an anti-Masonic paper. No source consulted explains the arrangement, and he never explained it either. What the columns contain is not denunciation but taxonomy: which bodies hold a real transmission, which are political clubs in aprons. He is building the distinction that organizes everything after, and he is building it in the pages of his enemies because they will print him.
suggested_refs: The Sphinx columns in La France antimaçonnique, from 1913

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne at last
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia for the baccalauréat ès arts at the Université de Paris, 1914-1917. The incoming pool gave 1912-1917, which is too early at the front end.
stops.campa: While Europe empties its universities into the trenches, Guénon, discharged and unfit, takes the arts degree at the Sorbonne that the collapse of 1905 denied him. Nine years late, and by the ordinary door rather than the competition. Around him the war is doing to the confidence of the European nineteenth century what he has been arguing on paper that a cycle does to itself at its end. He finishes the degree in 1917 and leaves France within months, for the first Muslim country he will live in.
suggested_refs: Université de Paris registers, baccalauréat ès arts 1914-1917

stops.name: Sétif, the year of teaching in Algeria
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedias for a one-year post, 1917-1918; the month is the ordinary start of the French school year and is inferred.
stops.campa: Guénon is sent to teach philosophy for a single year in the high plateau town of Sétif, in French Algeria: his first residence in a Muslim country, seven years after his initiation in Paris. Legend has wanted the decisive Sufi encounter to happen here. French Wikipedia refuses it outright and records that no contact with an Eastern master is documented for this stay. He teaches, he serves out the year, and he goes home. The refusal is worth more than the legend.
suggested_refs: Records of the collège at Sétif for the school year 1917-1918

stops.name: Paris, back on the island
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia for the return in 1918; the month is not recorded and is inferred from the end of the school year in Sétif.
stops.campa: He comes back to the Île Saint-Louis with a year of Algeria behind him and the war still running, thirty-one years old, unemployed, unplaceable, and in possession of a complete doctrine he has published nowhere but in a folded magazine. The next three years produce the book. From this point the biography stops being a list of societies joined and becomes a list of titles. He is still on the rue Saint-Louis-en-l'Île, and will keep the address another twelve years.
suggested_refs: Guénon's correspondence of 1918-1921, largely unpublished

stops.name: Paris, the rue Jacob and the first book
stops.date_confidence: attested by both Wikipedias for the publication year; the exact month is not recorded. The Marcel Rivière imprint on the rue Jacob is given by English Wikipedia.
stops.campa: Marcel Rivière, on the rue Jacob, publishes the Introduction générale à l'étude des doctrines hindoues. Guénon is thirty-four and this is his first book. The same year he publishes Le Théosophisme, histoire d'une pseudo-religion, four hundred pages taking apart Helena Blavatsky's society document by document, and begins appearing in the Revue de Philosophie. He arrives in French letters as two people at once: an expositor of the Vedanta and a prosecutor.
stops.quote: At its date, a book capital
stops.quote_source: André Malraux on the Introduction générale, quoted in Xavier Accart, René Guénon ou le renversement des clartés (2005), p. 76, via English Wikipedia
suggested_refs: Marcel Rivière, éditeur, rue Jacob, Paris VI, first edition of 1921

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne refuses the thesis
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia's Traditionalist School article that a thesis grounded in Hindu metaphysics was rejected and that he left the university in 1923. The article does not name the rejecting faculty; the Sorbonne pin follows where he studied, and is to that extent inference.
stops.campa: The doctoral thesis on Hindu metaphysics is refused, and Guénon leaves the university for the last time. He is thirty-six and has now been turned away by the French academy twice, at nineteen by his own body and at thirty-six by its judgment. The same year he publishes L'Erreur spirite, dismantling the seance rooms he sat in at twenty-one. Nothing he writes after this is written for a jury, and the prose changes accordingly: no hedging, no request for permission.
suggested_refs: The unpublished doctoral thesis of 1923, rejecting faculty unnamed in the sources consulted

stops.name: Paris, Orient et Occident
stops.date_confidence: attested 1924 by English Wikipedia's article on the book, which states it was originally published in 1924 in French. The incoming research pool dated it 1925, clustering it wrongly with two other events.
stops.campa: Orient et Occident appears: the argument that the West has lost the intellectual tradition the East still holds, and that no political or scientific remedy can touch the loss because the loss is metaphysical. The book proposes an elite of Westerners trained in Eastern doctrine to carry out a restoration. Guénon believes in the project when he writes it. Within three years he will stop believing in it, and the ship to Alexandria follows from that change of mind.
stops.quote: We are now in the fourth age, the Kali Yuga or 'dark age', and have been so already, it is said, for more than six thousand years, that is to say since a time far earlier than any known to 'classical' history.
stops.quote_source: The Crisis of the Modern World (1927), p. 7, English translation; verified via Wikiquote wikitext against the published edition
suggested_refs: Orient et Occident, first French edition, 1924

stops.name: Paris, Le Voile d'Isis
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the start of the collaboration in 1925. The coordinate is a placeholder: the editorial address of the review is not given in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Guénon begins writing for Le Voile d'Isis, Paul Chacornac's review, and slowly takes it over from the inside; under his influence it will be renamed Études Traditionnelles. It becomes the organ of a school that has no building, no membership, and no rites, only a common reading. He will still be filling its pages from Cairo twenty years later, correcting proofs by post across the Mediterranean, an editor in exile of a review he never formally edited.
stops.quote: It is contradictory to say that the same persons can be at the same time rulers and ruled ... The great ability of those who are in control in the modern world lies in making the people believe that they are governing themselves; and the people are the more inclined to believe this as they are flattered by it, and as, in any case, they are incapable of sufficient reflection to see its impossibility.
stops.quote_source: The Crisis of the Modern World (1927), p. 74, English translation; verified via Wikiquote wikitext
suggested_refs: Le Voile d'Isis, later Études Traditionnelles; editorial address unrecorded

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne lecture of 17 December
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by English Wikipedia for the lecture; L'Homme et son devenir selon le Vêdânta is attested to the year 1925 by both Wikipedias.
stops.campa: Two years after the same institution refused his thesis, Guénon stands in the Sorbonne and lectures. The Vedanta book has come out in the same year, the most purely expository thing he ever wrote, an account of the states of the human being that makes no polemical move at all. The hall he speaks in belongs to the university that would not have him. He is not being readmitted; he is being invited. He speaks in the hall, and goes back to the room on the island.
suggested_refs: Text or programme of the Sorbonne lecture of 17 December 1925

stops.name: Paris, La Crise du monde moderne
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication year 1927. The 'période charnière', the growing conviction that a Western restoration is impossible, is French Wikipedia's interpretive framing of the later 1920s and not a dated event; it is carried here as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The book that carries his name outside the specialist reviews. Guénon sets the whole of modernity inside the Hindu doctrine of cycles, names the age the Kali Yuga, and treats democracy, empirical science, and mass education as symptoms of one descent rather than as separate questions. It is also the book in which the hinge turns: the West he had proposed to help restore in 1924 is here past restoring. The next decision is geographic, and he takes three more years to make it.
stops.quote: 'Aristocracy' [...] taken in its etymological sense, means precisely the power of the elite. The elite can by definition only be the few, and their power, or rather their authority, deriving as it does from their intellectual superiority, has nothing in common with the numerical strength on which democracy is based, a strength whose inherent tendency is to sacrifice the minority to the majority, and therefore quality to quantity, and the elite to the masses.
stops.quote_source: The Crisis of the Modern World (1927), ch. 6 'Social Chaos', p. 78, English translation, Sophia Perennis edition; the elision marks words the incoming research pool had dropped silently
suggested_refs: La Crise du monde moderne, first French edition, 1927

stops.name: Paris, the deaths of 1928
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, not resolved. English Wikipedia dates the death of his wife Berthe Loury to 1928 and says it affected him deeply; French Wikipedia attaches a 1928 death to his aunt, Madame Duru. These are two different women and the sources are not reconciled here.
stops.campa: A death in 1928 empties the household on the island, and the sources do not agree whose it is. English Wikipedia buries Berthe Loury, the wife of sixteen years. French Wikipedia buries Madame Duru, the aunt who raised him, and notes that the visits to Montlivault stop in this year. Both may be true; neither source mentions the other's death. What is certain is that after 1928 there is nobody left in France that Guénon is obliged to stay for, and in 1930 he does not stay.
stops.quote: There can be only one way out of the chaos, in the social domain as in all others: the restoration of intellectuality, which would result in the formation once more of an elite.
stops.quote_source: The Crisis of the Modern World (1927), p. 79, English translation; verified via Wikiquote wikitext
suggested_refs: Civil death registers for Berthe Loury Guénon and for Madame Duru, 1928, not consulted in this pass

stops.name: Paris, Autorité spirituelle et pouvoir temporel
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the publication year 1929.
stops.campa: The last book of the French period sets out the doctrine of the two powers: the Brahmin and the Kshatriya, the priest and the king, knowledge above command and command legitimate only when it acknowledges what stands above it. Guénon reads the whole political history of Europe since the fourteenth century as the revolt of the second against the first, and traces it from Philip the Fair, who burned Jacques de Molay, forward to the parliaments. He is writing about hierarchy in the year the world's money collapses.
stops.quote: All temporal power that fails to recognize its subordination vis-à-vis spiritual authority is vain and illusory: separated from its principle, it can only exert itself in a disorderly way and move inexorably to its own ruin.
stops.quote_source: Spiritual Authority and Temporal Power (1929), translated by Henry D. Fohr (2001), pp. 28-29; verified via Wikiquote wikitext
suggested_refs: Autorité spirituelle et pouvoir temporel, first French edition, 1929

stops.name: Marseille, the embarkation for Egypt
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Both Wikipedias attest the departure for Egypt in September 1930; neither names a port, a ship, or a day. Marseille is the customary embarkation for Mediterranean steamers of the period and is inference, not record.
stops.campa: In September 1930 Guénon leaves France on what is announced as a research trip: some months in Egypt, manuscripts to be found, Sufi texts to be gathered for the review. He is forty-three, widowed or bereaved of the aunt or both, and carrying the conviction that the civilization he was born into cannot be repaired. No source consulted names the quay or the ship. He will never come back. The trip's stated purpose is not a lie; it is simply overtaken.
suggested_refs: Passenger manifests of the Marseille-Alexandria steamers, September 1930, not consulted

stops.name: Alexandria, the landfall
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The arrival in Egypt in September 1930 is attested; the port and the day are not. Alexandria is the standard landfall for the Marseille route and is used as the probable point of entry.
stops.campa: Egypt receives him at the ordinary port. Alexandria in 1930 is a Mediterranean city of Greeks, Italians, Jews, and Egyptians under a British occupation that will last another twenty-six years. Sixty-six years earlier the Emir Abdelkader was initiated into a Masonic lodge in this same city, and a hundred and thirty-two years earlier Bonaparte's fleet stood off this coast with a shipload of savants who invented Egyptology and, without meaning to, the Egyptian Rite Masonry Guénon grew up inside.
suggested_refs: Egyptian port entry records for September 1930, not consulted

stops.name: Cairo, the quarter of Khan el-Khalili
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for a seven-year residence in the medieval quarters from 1930; the month of settling is inferred from the September arrival.
stops.campa: Guénon takes rooms in the Fatimid city, among the coppersmiths and the booksellers of Khan el-Khalili, and not in the European quarters where a French writer of his standing would be expected. According to his biographer Paul Chacornac, his outward behaviour changes on arrival and he immerses himself entirely in the popular Islamic life of the city: the dress, the language, the hours of prayer. Ibn Battuta walked these lanes on the hajj road in 1326. The research trip quietly stops being a trip.
suggested_refs: Paul Chacornac, La Vie simple de René Guénon (1958; 2005 reprint), for the Cairo arrival

stops.name: Cairo, the courts of al-Azhar
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia in general terms for the 1930s; no course, teacher, or year is specified, so the anchor year is chosen and the attendance is undated in the source.
stops.campa: He attends lectures and sits in the circles of al-Azhar, a thousand years old and the working seat of Sunni learning, a Frenchman in a mosque-university reading in Arabic. He is not a convert seeking instruction in the elements; he has been Abd al-Wahid Yahya for twenty years and has published five books. What he takes from these courts is scholarship rather than initiation, the apparatus for the Islamic writing of the last two decades. The sentence below he had already written in Paris, four years earlier.
stops.quote: The truth is that there is really no 'profane realm' that could in any way be opposed to a 'sacred realm'; there is only a 'profane point of view', which is really none other than the point of view of ignorance.
stops.quote_source: The Crisis of the Modern World (1927), ch. 4 'Sacred and Profane Science', p. 53, Sophia Perennis English edition; Wikiquote misfiles this sentence under Initiation and Spiritual Realization (1952), and the incoming research pool inherited that error
suggested_refs: Al-Azhar mosque and university, Cairo; no attendance record traced

stops.name: Cairo, the mosque of Sayyidna al-Hussein
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the meeting with Sheikh Mohammad Ibrahim at this mosque; the source gives no year, and the anchor date is inference from the 1934 marriage that follows from the friendship.
stops.campa: At the shrine of Sayyidna al-Hussein, said to hold the head of the Prophet's grandson and one of the most visited places of prayer in Egypt, Guénon meets Sheikh Mohammad Ibrahim. The friendship is the hinge of the Cairo life. It is not a doctrinal encounter and no source presents it as one; it is two men who fall into conversation at a mosque, and it ends with the Frenchman married into the sheikh's household and buried in his city under an Arabic name.
suggested_refs: The mosque of Sayyidna al-Hussein, Cairo

stops.name: Cairo, the Hamidiyya Shadhiliyya zawiya
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout: the coordinate is approximate, the year is an anchor, and the association with the Hamidiyya branch of Sheikh Salama Hassan al-Radi is inference from English Wikipedia rather than a stated attendance.
stops.campa: The Shadhili order, into which Aguéli brought him in Paris around 1910, is a living institution here with buildings and a living shaykh: Salama Hassan al-Radi, whose Hamidiyya branch is one of the largest in Egypt. Cairo consolidates an affiliation rather than beginning one. English Wikipedia elsewhere dates the whole initiation to 1930 and to a man dead since 1917; the claim fails on arithmetic. The chain he entered runs back to Ibn Arabi at Damascus.
suggested_refs: The Hamidiyya Shadhiliyya zawiya of Sheikh Salama Hassan al-Radi, Cairo; the actual zawiya frequented is unrecorded

stops.name: Cairo, the marriage to Fatima Ibrahim
stops.date_confidence: the marriage in 1934 and the four children are attested by English Wikipedia; the site of the ceremony is not given in any source consulted, and the old-city pin near Sayyidna al-Hussein is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Guénon marries Fatima, daughter of Sheikh Mohammad Ibrahim. He is forty-seven, and the marriage on the island in 1912 produced no children; this one produces four. The Frenchman who spent twenty-five years arguing that the West had lost the transmission its cathedrals were built on is now a son-in-law in an Egyptian Sufi family, with a household and a language he was not born to. Fifteen years later the state will issue him the papers to match. The wedding place itself the sources do not record.
suggested_refs: Egyptian civil and religious marriage records, 1934, not consulted in this pass

stops.name: Mecca, the qibla he never travels to
stops.date_confidence: not a visit and not attested as one. Guénon is nowhere recorded performing the hajj. This pin is the canonical Kaaba coordinate carried by the corpus, inherited unchanged, and marks the direction of his prayer for twenty-one years rather than a journey.
stops.campa: Five times a day in Dokki and in Khan el-Khalili, Abd al-Wahid Yahya turns his body toward a point in the Hijaz he will never see. Pilgrims by the millions have circled that stone across fourteen centuries, on foot and on camel and by ship and by plane. Guénon does not make the journey; the roughly thirteen hundred kilometres between Cairo and Mecca are never crossed by him in either direction. The orientation is in the life all the same, and a record that maps only footsteps would miss it.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba, Mecca; carried here as the qibla of the Cairo years, not as a stop travelled
sources: canonical corpus pin, inherited from abdelkader.journey.json, hallaj.journey.json and ibn_battuta.journey.json

stops.name: Cairo, the house in Dokki
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia for the acquisition in 1937 and the name Villa Fatima; the street address is not given. English Wikipedia's added phrase 'at the foot of the pyramids' is false and is dropped: Dokki is an inner-city district on the west bank, some ten kilometres from Giza.
stops.campa: The family crosses the Nile west to Dokki and takes a house named Villa Fatima, bought with help from the English disciple John Levy. Guénon lives here fourteen years and hardly leaves it. Letters go out by the hundred to Europe and America, articles go to Paris for Études Traditionnelles, visitors are received sparingly and by appointment. The books of the last fourteen years are written in this villa, in longhand, by a man who has stopped travelling.
stops.quote: The 'end of a world' never is and never can be anything but the end of an illusion.
stops.quote_source: The Reign of Quantity and the Signs of the Times (1945), translated by Lord Northbourne (1953); verified via Wikiquote wikitext
suggested_refs: Villa Fatima, Dokki, Cairo; street address unrecorded and the building's present condition unestablished

stops.name: Cairo, Schuon arrives from Mulhouse
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia's article on Frithjof Schuon for a first in-person meeting in Egypt in 1938 after seven years of correspondence; the article does not state that the meeting took place at Villa Fatima, so the location is inference.
stops.campa: Frithjof Schuon, who has been writing to Guénon from Mulhouse since 1931, comes to Egypt and meets him for the first time. The Traditionalist school acquires its second man. It will acquire more, and it will fracture: Schuon eventually claims a spiritual authority of his own that Guénon does not concede, and the two drift apart before the war ends. Ananda Coomaraswamy, nine years the elder and no man's disciple, is meanwhile saying this in print in Boston.
stops.quote: No living writer in modern Europe is more significant than René Guénon, whose task it has been to expound the universal metaphysical tradition that has been the essential foundation of every past culture, and which represents the indispensable basis for any civilization deserving to be so called.
stops.quote_source: Ananda Coomaraswamy, introduction to his translation of part of La crise du monde moderne, quoted in Roger Lipsey, Coomaraswamy, vol. 3: His Life and Work (1977), p. 169; via Wikiquote wikitext
suggested_refs: The Guénon-Schuon correspondence, 1931-1938

stops.name: Cairo, Schuon on the way to India
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia's Schuon article for a long Cairo stopover in 1939 en route to India with two disciples; the month is not given and the meeting place is again inferred to be Villa Fatima.
stops.campa: Schuon breaks a voyage to India at Cairo and sees Guénon again, this time with two followers of his own. It is among the last recorded meetings between them. Within months Europe is at war, the sea lanes close, and the correspondence that built the school has to cross a Mediterranean full of submarines. Guénon spends the war in Dokki writing Le Règne de la Quantité, which argues that the disaster now visible everywhere is not a rupture in the cycle but its ordinary late weather.
suggested_refs: Schuon's 1939 Indian voyage and its Cairo stopover

stops.name: Vatican City, Maritain asks for the Index
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the year within an attested window. English Wikipedia says the request came after the Second World War, when Jacques Maritain was French Ambassador to the Vatican; Maritain held that post from 1945 to 1948. The incoming research pool dated it 1940, which the same source contradicts.
stops.campa: Jacques Maritain, Catholic philosopher and now France's ambassador to the Holy See, judges Guénon's doctrines radically irreconcilable with the faith and asks that his works be entered on the Index of Prohibited Books. Pius XII refuses and nothing is listed. The most systematic living defender of spiritual authority against temporal power is denounced to the oldest spiritual authority in Europe, and it declines to move against him. Elsewhere the reading of him runs stranger still.
stops.quote: Carl Schmitt believes Rene Guenon is the most interesting person of our time. (I don't believe this always, but often I do. Although I consider Aurobindo Ghose more 'perfected.')
stops.quote_source: Mircea Eliade, The Portugal Journal, translated by Mac Linscott Ricketts (2010), written at Lisbon in the war years; via Wikiquote wikitext
suggested_refs: Records of the Congregation of the Holy Office concerning the Maritain request, 1945-1948

stops.name: Cairo, Egyptian citizenship
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia gives 1949; French Wikipedia gives a range of 1948-1951. Both are retained and neither is preferred on evidence. The office where the naturalization was processed is not identified, and the pin is central Cairo as a placeholder.
stops.campa: Nineteen years after stepping off a boat for a few months' research, Guénon becomes an Egyptian. The paper catches up with a fact settled long before: a Cairo household, four children, an Arabic name in daily use since 1910, a French passport that had become a technicality. He is sixty-two. Everything he has published for twenty years has gone to France, under his own name, from a man who has not lived there since 1930. No French institution ever employed him longer than the school year at Sétif.
suggested_refs: Egyptian naturalization records, 1948-1951, not consulted in this pass

stops.name: Cairo, death at Villa Fatima
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by both Wikipedias. The single word 'Allah' is quoted from Chacornac through English Wikipedia; the surrounding clause is Wikipedia's own narration and is not quoted here as Chacornac's.
stops.campa: On Sunday the seventh of January, in the house in Dokki, René Guénon dies at sixty-four. Twenty-two volumes will eventually carry his name in English alone; in his lifetime he had readers in the hundreds and correspondents on four continents, and not one chair, prize, or degree. The cause of death and the course of the last illness are not detailed in any source consulted. What the sources do carry is the last word, and it is in the language of the city he chose rather than the one he was born to.
stops.quote_source: Guénon's last word, according to his biographer Paul Chacornac, La Vie simple de René Guénon (1958; 2005 reprint), p. 98, as reported by English Wikipedia
suggested_refs: Chacornac's account of the death of 7 January 1951

stops.name: Cairo, the grave in the necropolis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and an open gap. Neither Wikipedia names any cemetery. Secondary web accounts point to the al-Darrasa sector on the edge of the old walls, and the pin follows that reading at roughly 30.050, 31.266; the incoming research pool carried two mutually exclusive coordinates four kilometres apart. The burial day is inferred from Muslim practice.
stops.campa: He is buried in Cairo by Muslim rite, as Abd al-Wahid Yahya, the day after his death or close to it. Where, exactly, no reachable source will say. The accounts point vaguely at the Qarafa, the necropolis that has been a working neighbourhood of the living for a thousand years, and visitors report finding the stone by chance if at all. One marker stands here instead of two, and the case states plainly: the cemetery is unidentified, the plot unverified, and no photograph of the grave was located.
suggested_refs: Egyptian burial registers for January 1951; the cemetery remains unnamed in every source reached
sources: English Wikipedia, 'City of the Dead (Cairo)' for the al-Darrasa geography

stops.name: Paris, the shelves that outlive him
stops.date_confidence: the counts are attested by French Wikipedia; the anchor date is an arbitrary point in the year of his death. The Gide remark is dated 1951 by Wikiquote, which cites a personal web page, and is the weakest citation in this file.
stops.campa: Seventeen books published in his lifetime, ten posthumous collections of articles, twenty-seven titles kept in print. Éditions Traditionnelles holds the historic catalogue; Gallimard later takes eleven titles and adds the critical apparatus he would have refused. Manuscripts and letters are said to be lodged in part at the Bibliothèque Nationale, though this report obtained no shelfmark. In Paris in the year he dies, André Gide, who built a life on the opposite premise, is reported saying this.
stops.quote: Si Guenon a raison, eh bien! toute mon oeuvre tombe.
stops.quote_source: André Gide, 1951, as quoted at 'Pourquoi lire Guenon aujourd'hui?' (membres.multimania.fr/aziyade), reproduced via Wikiquote wikitext; translates as 'If Guenon is right, well, all my work collapses'
suggested_refs: Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Guénon papers; holdings asserted by secondary sources, no catalogue record obtained

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the southern readership
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Borges's residence in Buenos Aires is attested in borges.journey.json; that file does not mention Guénon, and the reception claim is outside-corpus knowledge. The anchor year is arbitrary.
stops.campa: Guénon never crosses the Atlantic and never learns Spanish well enough to be read in it. Buenos Aires reads him anyway. Jorge Luis Borges, working the same material of cyclical time and of a knowledge older than the books that carry it, cites the Frenchman's doctrine in his essays, and Argentine esoteric circles take up the Traditionalist argument with an appetite Paris never had. He has no institution anywhere to carry him, and the readership assembles somewhere he never went.
suggested_refs: Borges's essayistic references to Guénon; the Argentine Traditionalist reception
sources: borges.journey.json (canonical Buenos Aires pin, inherited unchanged)

stops.name: Madrid, the complete Spanish edition
stops.date_confidence: attested by Spanish Wikipedia for April 2023, twenty-three volumes plus an introductory volume, edited by Javier Alvarado Planas of the UNED. Madrid is the university's seat and stands here for the edition rather than for a printing house address.
stops.campa: Seventy-two years after the death in Dokki, the complete works appear in Spanish in twenty-three volumes with an introductory twenty-fourth, edited by a professor of history at the UNED. The English collected works had been finished in New York, the French catalogue split between two houses, and now the language of the Buenos Aires readership gets the whole thing at once. A man who published his first mature thought in a magazine with no subscribers ends up in uniform bindings in four languages.
suggested_refs: Obras completas de René Guénon, ed. Javier Alvarado Planas, 24 vols., April 2023
